per_run.approach_summary: Profiled all 200 continuous features and compared distributed linear models, full and screened random forests/ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost using five-fold stratified cross-validation. The signal was broad and mostly linear in research CV: shrinkage LDA scored 0.8412 and strongly regularized logistic regression 0.8396, versus 0.8056 for LightGBM, 0.8148 for CatBoost, 0.7775 for ExtraTrees, and 0.7555 for random forest; feature screening did not improve ExtraTrees. Confirmation feedback showed useful distribution-specific nonlinear complementarity: LDA scored 0.8009, logistic 0.7981, LightGBM 0.8004, and ExtraTrees 0.7843. Rank blending improved materially; tested LDA/LightGBM blends and three-model blends, with the best confirmation AUC 0.8202 from weights 0.40 shrinkage LDA, 0.40 LightGBM, and 0.20 full-feature ExtraTrees. Transfer predictions use that rank ensemble, fit on all 5000 research rows.

Profiled all 200 numeric features, including univariate discrimination and sequential prevalence stability. Compared five-fold stratified CV for standardized regularized logistic regression, extremely randomized trees, and LightGBM; CV AUCs were approximately 0.828, 0.794, and 0.837. Used 20 permitted confirmation calls to test L1/L2 regularization, univariate feature selection, shallow and deeper boosting, CatBoost, and rank ensembles. Confirmation rejected aggressive feature selection and favored nonlinear models: the strongest single LightGBM scored 0.8217, while complementary linear and CatBoost rankings improved robustness. The selected final predictor is a rank ensemble of 40% LightGBM (15 leaves), 40% CatBoost (depth 6), and 20% L2 logistic regression (C=0.03), trained on all 5,000 research rows; it achieved the best confirmation AUC of 0.8308.

Profiled all 200 continuous features, including cardinality, missingness, univariate AUC, mutual information, and target stability by row-id segment. The signal was broad and additive: regularized logistic regression reached 0.8344 shuffled-CV AUC, while nonlinear models captured complementary structure (LightGBM 0.8317 and CatBoost 0.8238; tree/logistic blends reached about 0.8487). Confirmation exposed a generalization difference: logistic scored 0.7933 versus 0.8265 for cross-fitted LightGBM, so final tuning emphasized cross-fitted, regularized boosting. Shallow and medium LightGBM variants were tested across tree counts; confirmation peaked at 0.8279 individually, 0.8290 for a rank blend of 15-leaf/800-tree and 31-leaf/400-tree models, and 0.8337 after adding cross-fitted CatBoost. Final transfer predictions use that three-model rank ensemble, which is insensitive to calibration drift and preserves the complementary ordering.

Explored all 200 anonymized features with univariate diagnostics, row-order prevalence checks, regularized logistic regression, shrinkage LDA, ExtraTrees/random forests, histogram boosting, Gaussian naive Bayes, and correlation-ranked feature subsets. The signal was broadly distributed and predominantly linear: 5-fold shuffled CV AUC was about 0.841 for strongly regularized ridge logistic and shrinkage LDA, versus 0.771 for ExtraTrees. A 120-feature screen reached 0.847 in shuffled CV but only 0.7990 confirmation AUC, evidence that its apparent gain was partly selection overfit. All-feature ridge and automatic-shrinkage LDA scored 0.8001 and 0.8009 on confirmation. Rank blending LDA, ridge, and a small 120-feature component scored 0.8012. Gaussian naive Bayes alone scored 0.7941 but supplied complementary ranking; a conservative 40% Gaussian / 60% linear-ensemble rank blend scored 0.8076 and is used for transfer. I attacked the best approach as potentially exploiting random folds, row order, unstable feature selection, or confirmation-specific distribution. Contiguous 1000-row held-out blocks gave overall AUC 0.8348 (individual blocks 0.8229-0.8588), target prevalence was stable across row blocks, and maximum standardized feature-mean shifts from research were only 0.102 for confirmation and 0.090 for transfer. The attack rejected the feature-subset-only winner but found no convincing regime or transfer-shift failure for the regularized all-feature ensemble; hence the subset remains low-weight and the final prediction uses robust rank averaging.

Loaded all 200 numeric features and profiled marginal AUC, mutual information, cardinality, missingness, and research/confirmation/transfer shifts. Compared five-fold out-of-fold logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM variants, feature-selected boosting, and CatBoost. Local AUCs included 0.8247 logistic, 0.7810 ExtraTrees, 0.8257 baseline LightGBM, 0.8257 deeper LightGBM, and 0.8031/0.7477 CatBoost depth 6/8. Confirmation scores showed boosted trees generalized best: baseline LightGBM 0.8270, deeper LightGBM 0.8296, while logistic and ExtraTrees scored 0.7916 and 0.8007. Rank blends were stable around 0.830; the final blend uses 30% baseline LightGBM, 45% deeper regularized LightGBM, and 25% depth-8 CatBoost and scored 0.8309. I deliberately attacked the result as a possible confirmation artifact. There were no exact row duplicates, row ID had only 0.519 research AUC with broadly stable decile prevalence, and a classifier separating research from confirmation had cross-validated AUC 0.495, providing no evidence of confirmation-specific covariate structure. The attack did identify genuine selection overfit: globally selecting the top 100 LightGBM features raised apparent local AUC to 0.8455 but fell to 0.8089 on confirmation (top 50 fell to 0.7603), so I rejected all selected-feature models. The retained all-feature ensemble was robust across algorithms and nearby blend weights (0.8298-0.8309), although the CatBoost component trades lower local AUC for useful ranking diversity.

I profiled all 200 continuous features and compared regularized logistic regression, shrinkage LDA, ExtraTrees, CatBoost, Gaussian naive Bayes, and rank blends using stratified out-of-fold AUC. The broad independent-distribution signal was clearest: Gaussian naive Bayes achieved about 0.862 CV AUC, versus about 0.846 for LDA, 0.839 for logistic regression, and 0.798 for ExtraTrees. Confirmation scoring agreed: GNB scored 0.8409, while LDA and logistic scored 0.8009 and 0.7938; blends were worse. I tested variance/mean shrinkage and robustly clipping each feature's Gaussian log-likelihood-ratio contribution. A clip of 1 improved confirmation AUC to 0.8422 (nearby clips 0.8, 1.2, and 1.5 scored 0.8415, 0.8419, and 0.8418), so the final model fits class-specific means and variances on all research rows, clips each feature contribution to [-1,1], sums them, and applies a monotone tempered sigmoid. I attacked this result as potentially confirmation-specific by checking sequential row IDs, duplicates, feature-distribution shifts, feature correlations, contiguous row-block validation, and multiple shuffled CV seeds. There were no duplicate rows; confirmation and transfer had similarly small standardized mean/variance shifts; feature correlations were low; contiguous CV remained 0.856 and shuffled-seed CV was about 0.855-0.862. Thus I found no convincing split artifact or spurious-feature explanation and retained the robust clipped model.

STRUCTURE FOUND. The 200 features are mutually near-independent (max |pairwise corr| = 0.063) and ~167/200 carry weak individual signal (univariate AUC 0.42-0.58; mean univariate chi-square 6.2 vs 1.0 under the null). A capacity-matched L2 logistic regression got 5x5-fold CV AUC 0.839 and LightGBM 0.839 -- trees cannot aggregate 200 tiny independent additive effects, so they land in the same place as the linear model.

The real structure is a single SHARED, STRONGLY CONVEX per-feature response curve. Evidence: (a) a score test for x^2 terms after the linear fit gave 11 features with |z|>3 (0.5 expected) and EVERY one of them positive, with the curvature magnitude correlated 0.49 with |linear coefficient| -- the signature of log-odds = sum_j a_j * h(s_j * z_j) with a_j>0, s_j = +-1 and one common convex h (not of sum_j c_j*h(z_j), which would give curvature signs following c_j); (b) pooled partial residuals against the sign-oriented z-score are flat-to-negative up to about +1 SD and then rise sharply (+0.038 in the top bin). Estimating h nonparametrically on a hinge basis, weighted by feature importance, gives a curve that is nearly flat below z=+1, ramps steeply between +1.0 and +2.0 SD, and continues rising more gently above. An exponential surrogate exp(0.8*z) already captures most of it (CV 0.870); the fitted nonparametric shape reaches 0.875.

MECHANISM. Because h is essentially a tail-weighted ramp, the target is driven by how many features sit in their upper signed tail. An UNWEIGHTED count of features with oriented z > 1.5 (mean count 13.8 of 200) alone scores AUC 0.834, nearly matching the full 200-coefficient logistic regression: P(y=1) climbs monotonically from 0.003 (count<=8) through 0.030 (count 13) to 0.425 (count>=19). The signal is a diffuse excess of upper-tail deviations spread across the whole feature set, not a handful of drivers.

WHAT I RULED OUT. Pairwise interactions: a full 19,900-pair score test found 0 pairs with |z|>4 (1.25 expected by chance) and max |z| = 3.59 -- fewer extremes than chance, so the model is purely additive. Per-feature shape heterogeneity: adding ridge-shrunk per-feature spline deviations on top of the pooled shape degraded CV monotonically as the shrinkage was relaxed (0.874 -> 0.861), i.e. the response curve is genuinely COMMON to all 200 features. Scale: the effect lives in per-feature standardized units, not raw units (a rate parameterization c*sd^(1-gamma) peaked cleanly at gamma=1). Rank-gaussianizing the features HURT (0.870 -> 0.864), so the raw linear scale is the right one. Subpopulations / covariate shift: research vs confirmation vs transfer marginals agree (max mean-shift |z| = 3.5 over 200 features, as expected for IID sampling), and a score x feature modulation test found max |z| = 2.69 over 200 tests -- no subpopulation structure. After fitting, residual score tests for linear, quadratic, exponential, hinge and pairwise terms all sit at chance, so the model is well specified and the remaining error is estimation noise, not misspecification.

FINAL MODEL. Sign-orient each feature by its exponential-space marginal association; estimate one pooled shape h on a hinge basis (importance-weighted pooling across features, ridge-regularized); then re-estimate per-feature weights marginally (valid because the features are independent -- this beat joint ridge at every penalty) and clip them at >=0 (all true a_j are non-negative). Ensembled over 12 configurations (4 knot vectors x 3 orientation bandwidths) by rank averaging, then blended 0.9/0.1 with a LightGBM for diversity. 5-fold CV over 3 seeds: 0.8754.

CONFIRMATION FEEDBACK (4 calls). Linear-logistic baseline 0.7981; pooled-shape ensemble 0.8556 / 0.8544; final 0.9/0.1 blend 0.8551. The +0.057 gap between the linear baseline and the shape model on held-out confirmation rows is larger than the +0.035 gap seen in CV, so the discovered structure transfers rather than being a CV artifact. All confirmation scores run about 0.02 below their CV counterparts -- a uniform level offset on this particular 1500-row draw (its ~157 positives give an AUC standard error near 0.017), and the ordering of models is preserved. Because the confirmation set cannot separate variants only 0.0005 apart, I selected the final model on the far more precise 3-seed CV rather than on confirmation, and used confirmation only to verify that the structural gain was real.

STRUCTURE FOUND. 200 anonymized continuous features, 5000 labeled rows, 10.5% positive. First pass: the feature correlation matrix is indistinguishable from identity (max |r|=0.045 over 19900 pairs; eigenspectrum matches Marchenko-Pastur), so the features are mutually independent -- there is no latent factor structure to recover. Every one of the 200 features is platykurtic (excess kurtosis -0.83..-0.06, skew ~0); per-feature 2-component Gaussian mixtures fit with weights ~0.50/0.50 and separation 1.6-2.6 noise-sd, i.e. each feature carries an independent latent 50/50 bit. I chased that encoding hard and it was a dead end for prediction: soft-bit posteriors alone gave CV AUC 0.803 vs 0.839 for raw values, and a full scan of all 19900 bit-pair products against the linear model's residual found max |corr| 0.0596 against a null max of ~0.0566 -- no XOR/parity/interaction structure. The mixture is how the features were generated, not where the signal lives.

The signal is an ADDITIVE LOCATION-SCALE effect. Scanning squared/abs terms against the linear residual gave max |corr| 0.080 vs null max 0.049 (22 features with |z|>3), while continuous pairwise interactions gave 0.058 vs null 0.065 -- curvature but no interactions. The curvature is positive regardless of the sign of the linear effect, which pointed at a variance effect, and it is: positives have inflated per-feature variance on 157/200 features (mean var ratio 1.066, mean log-ratio z=+0.94, zero features significantly deflated). sum(z^2) alone scores AUC 0.726. So the classes differ in BOTH location and scale, and under conditional independence the Bayes rule is exactly additive: sum_j log f1_j/f0_j, quadratic-ish per feature. That explains why trees do badly here (LGBM 0.841, depth-1 additive boosting 0.802): the signal is a weak, dense, smooth additive effect spread over all 200 features, which is the worst case for axis-aligned splits.

I tested and REJECTED the subpopulation hypothesis that first suggested itself. |mean shift| correlates 0.48 with variance inflation, which is what you would see if the positive class were a mixture of clusters with different mean-shift vectors. That makes a sharp prediction: positives should show excess feature correlation. They do not -- correlation sd among positives is 0.0438 vs a null of 0.0437, and their correlation eigenspectrum matches negatives subsampled to the same n almost exactly. Positives are conditionally independent given the class; the mean/variance correlation is just the induced signature of convex per-feature shape functions.

MODEL. The winning move was exploiting that the scale effect is nearly UNIFORM across features (optimal shrinkage of feature-specific log-variance-ratios toward their common mean was lam_v=0.2, and adding a feature-specific variance block to the pooled model cost ~0.012 AUC). That licenses pooling shape estimation across all 200 features: logit = a*sum_j phi(z_j) + sum_j w_j*psi(z_j) with phi, psi shared spline shapes (18 parameters total) and w_j the per-feature mean difference. The learned shapes came out as phi ~ z^2 (corr 0.973) and psi ~ z (corr 0.984), both with mild tail steepening -- exactly the density ratio of two shifted/scaled mixture distributions. Final model is an equal-weight rank average of three members: this pooled shared-shape model (3 knot settings), a shrunken naive-Bayes location-scale density ratio (2 settings), and a lin+quad+cubic penalized logistic. Research OOF (4x5-fold) 0.8751; fully NESTED CV with all hyperparameters and blend weights chosen inside the outer fold 0.8697, vs 0.8422 for penalized linear logistic and 0.8414 for tuned LGBM. Things that did NOT help: orthogonalized polynomial bases (0.857 -- the raw power basis's L2 penalty is a better smoothness prior), rank-gauss (0.867), soft-thresholding the weights (0.862, so the effect is dense, not sparse), and joint/EM re-estimation of w with the scale part as an offset (0.863 -- the plain mean difference is already the efficient estimator under conditional independence).

CONFIRMATION (7 calls). Final blend 0.8496; penalized linear 0.7994; quadratic-only 0.7304. The blend-over-linear margin was LARGER on confirmation (+0.050) than in CV (+0.033), so the location-scale structure is not a research-set artifact.

SELF-ATTACK. The strongest case against my model was a real anomaly I found in my own numbers: bootstrapping 1500-row subsamples of the research OOF, the confirmation score for the linear model (0.7994) sits at the 0.05th percentile -- a drop far outside sampling noise -- while quadratic-only (0.7304 vs 0.7364 expected) sits at the 36th percentile, i.e. it transfers perfectly. The natural reading is that the mean-shift vector delta drifts between the research and confirmation regions while the variance inflation is stable, which would mean my model leans too hard on the linear part and would transfer badly. I attacked this four ways. (1) Row_ids are sequential blocks (research 0-4999, confirmation 5000-6499, transfer 6500-7999), so I tested for drift WITHIN research using contiguous-block CV: 0.8397 vs 0.8379 for random-split CV on the linear part, 0.7272 vs 0.7304 on the quadratic -- no drift. (2) delta estimated on research rows 0-2499 vs 2500-4999 correlates 0.716, statistically identical to random halves (0.733 +- 0.027) and to the 0.761 expected if delta were perfectly stable. (3) I mapped the linear/scale trade-off curve explicitly: the research-optimal mixing weight is lam=0.70, and probing confirmation at lam=0.50/0.70/0.85 gave 0.8345/0.8418/0.8321 -- confirmation peaks at lam=0.70, EXACTLY the research optimum. That is the decisive result: if delta had drifted, confirmation would have preferred a lower lam. It did not, so I did NOT reweight, and the linear model's low score is a genuinely unlucky draw rather than structural drift. (4) Other exploit routes checked and closed: no near-duplicate leakage (nearest-neighbour distance from confirmation to research rows, 15.16 min / 16.94 median, is identical to research-to-research); no distribution shift (adversarial validation AUC 0.5035 research-vs-transfer, and per-row RMS |z| is 0.9992/0.9988/0.9987 across the three splits); transductive preprocessing contributes nothing (0.8696 using all 8000 rows vs 0.8698 using research rows only), so the score does not depend on having seen the confirmation/transfer features. My model selection was driven by research CV throughout -- the confirmation calls were used to validate and to run the lam probe, and that probe resulted in no change to the model.

HEADROOM. Simulating the fitted location-scale model (deconvolving estimation noise: true mean delta^2 = 0.0123, var ratio 1.066) gives Bayes-optimal AUC 0.871 under a Gaussian approximation, dropping to 0.854 when delta is estimated from only 524 positives. My confirmation score of 0.8496 sits essentially at that realistic ceiling, and my OOF exceeds the Gaussian-approximation Bayes rate because the real features are mixtures, whose shifted density ratio is more informative in the shoulders than a Gaussian's -- which is precisely the tail steepening the pooled shape model learned. The binding constraint is irreducible: estimating a dense 200-dimensional mean shift from 524 positives. Residual scans after the final blend confirm nothing is left (linear 0.031 and pairwise 0.059 both below their null maxima; quadratic 0.0558 vs null max 0.0490 is ~1 SD of the max distribution and corresponds to the feature-specific variance term I already tested and rejected because it cost CV AUC).
